newsitem.title: SIERRA LEONE: Sierra Leone coup leaders said to want $46 million.
newsitem.headline: Sierra Leone coup leaders said to want $46 million.

text.p: Leaders of a coup in Sierra Leone are demanding $46 million to step down and allow the return of ousted civilian president Ahmad Tejan Kabbah, sources close to the coup leaders said on Tuesday.

Sierra Leone's ambassador to the United Nations, James Jonah, said on Monday the coup leaders wanted money to give up power, but Director of Defence Information Colonel Abdul Sesay denied the allegation.
"There have been no negotiations concerning money," Sesay told Reuters.
Sesay said there had been no contacts since negotiations involving British and Nigerian diplomats and civilian politicians broke down on June 1, the eve of a Nigerian naval bombardment of Freetown.
He said the Armed Forces Revolutionary Council hoped to get the talks back on track to settle the crisis amicably.
"The coup leaders and their rebel allies are now demanding $46 million to step down to allow the return of President Ahmad Tejan Kabbah," said one source.
He said the sum would be shared between a total of about 35 soldiers and rebels of the Revolutionary United Front (RUF) who have allied with the army since the May 25 coup.

Sources close to the talks said that in earlier negotiations with the coupmakers, Nigerian diplomats and military officials offered them $10,000 each, a car and a house in any part of Nigeria. The soldiers and rebels turned the Nigerian offer down.
"They asked for monetary payment," Jonah told reporters in New York, without mentioning a sum.
"And they want 18 months in office to loot further. That is all they want to do. It is just shameful."

Jonah said Kabbah had sent a letter to Nigerian head of state General Sani Abacha, with a copy to U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan, saying he accepted a deal that would grant amnesty to the coup leaders, and look at grievances in the army and other demands.
Jonah said the coup leaders had agreed to many terms but their RUF allies had refused. He accused the military and the RUF of planning killings of civilian opponents of the military.

"The junta and the RUF are planning genocide in the event of what they consider (military) intervention. In light of the experience in Rwanda...I met with the Security Council president to issue a warning on this," Jonah said.
Sesay said there was no question of genocide. "It is not true. That's not our intention."

He said that when the coupmakers first invited the RUF to join them, they themselves were afraid of the RUF fighters committing atrocities. "But from our talks with the RUF we now know they are genuinely committed to peace," he said.
"James Jonah is not a patriot, he is not a true Sierra Leonean, otherwise he would not be supporting armed intervention in what he calls his country," Sesay said.
He said Kabbah had been trying to contact the military leaders through political opposition leader John Karefa-Smart but there had been no direct contact so far.
The coup is causing increasing hardship to Freetown residents. Petrol and staple foods are scarce and expensive, banks and businesses are still closed and May's salaries have not been paid.
Callers to a phone-in programme on private radio WBIG (We Believe in God) on Monday night called on Major Johnny Paul Koroma to step down. "People are frustrated by the hardship," a caller said.
Callers praised him for achieving peace in the six-year war against the RUF, but warned him not to ignore their suffering and the threat of military intervention.
